text: Isa Genzken, born on 27 November 1948, is a German artist who lives and works in Berlin. Her primary media are sculpture and installation, utilizing a wide range of materials such as concrete, plaster, wood, and textile, as well as photography, video, film, and collage. Raised mostly in Bad Oldesloe and Hamburg, she studied fine arts and art history with Almir Mavignier and Kai Sudeck at the Hamburg University of Fine Arts (1968–1971) and the Berlin University of the Arts (1971–1973), working part-time as a model to cover tuition costs. In 1973, she transferred to the Arts Academy Düsseldorf while studying art history and philosophy at the University of Cologne, where fellow students included Katharina Fritsch and Thomas Struth. After graduating in 1977, she taught sculpture at the academy. She married Gerhard Richter in 1982 and moved to Cologne in 1983, separating from him in 1993 and returning to Berlin. Genzken has bipolar disorder, experiences manic and depressive phases, and has been hospitalized in psychiatric facilities; she has also undergone treatment for substance abuse, stating in a 2016 interview that her alcohol issues began after her divorce and that she had been sober since 2013. She has worked in studios in Düsseldorf, Cologne (designed in 1993 by architect Frank Tebroke), for short periods in Lower Manhattan and Hoboken, New Jersey, and currently in Berlin. Although her primary focus is sculpture, she has produced works in photography, film, video, works on paper, oil paintings, collages, collage books, film scripts, and even a record. Her practice draws on Constructivism and Minimalism and engages critically with Modernist architecture and contemporary visual and material culture, maintaining traditional sculpture conventions while incorporating plaster, cement, building samples, photographs, and bric-a-brac to create architectonic structures described as contemporary ruins. She uses mirrors and reflective surfaces to involve viewers physically and spatially, and employs placement methods to evoke emotional responses by requiring viewers to move around her works. The column is a recurring motif, representing a "pure" architectural element to explore the relationship between high art and mass-produced popular culture. In the 1970s, she began working with wood, carving unusual geometric forms such as hyperboloids and ellipsoids; her Hi-Fi-Serie (1979) reproduces stereo phonograph advertisements. In 1980, she and Richter were commissioned to design the König-Heinrich-Platz underground station in Duisburg, completed in 1992. Between 1986 and 1992, she created a series of plaster and concrete sculptures with sequentially poured and stacked slabs featuring rough openings, windows, and interiors. A later series includes epoxy resin casts of architectural or interior elements, such as columns or lamps. In 1986, her architectural references shifted from the 1910s–1930s to the 1950s–1970s. In 1990, she installed Camera (1990) on a Brussels gallery's rooftop. In 2000, she produced a series of patched-together architectural models inscribed with "Fuck the Bauhaus," and in the series New Buildings for Berlin, shown at Documenta 11, she designed glass high-rise visions. The project Der Spiegel 1989–1991 consists of 121 black-and-white photographs from the German newsweekly Der Spiegel, cut and glued to white card, mounted in simple frames with dates providing contextual clues. Her MLR (More Light Research) (1992) paintings of suspended hoops recall gymnastics apparatus frozen mid-swing. From 1995 to 1996, while in New York, she created the three-volume collage book I Love New York, Crazy City, compiling souvenirs such as photographs, maps, hotel bills, nightclub flyers, and concert tickets. One of her most recognized works, Rose (1993/7), is an eight-meter-tall public sculpture of a single long-stemmed rose made from enamelled stainless steel, installed at the Leipzig fairgrounds; her first public artwork in the United States, Rose II (2007), was installed outside the New Museum as part of a rotating installation in November 2010. She has produced numerous films, including Zwei Frauen im Gefecht (1974), Chicago Drive (1992), Meine Großeltern im Bayerischen Wald (1992), and Empire/Vampire, Who Kills Death (2003). She has published five portfolio-style books, available through David Zwirner's Books website, including Sculpture as a World Receiver, October Files, Isa Genzken: Retrospective, Isa Genzken: Oil, and Isa Genzken. Since the late 1990s, she has conceptualized sculptures and panel paintings in the form of bricolage, using materials from DIY stores and photographs and newspaper clippings, often emphasizing the temporary nature of her works. Her interest in urban space is evident in complex, disquieting installations featuring mannequins, dolls, photographs, and found objects. New Buildings for New York is assembled from found plastic, metal, and pizza-box cardboard. The Empire/Vampire, Who Kills Death series, created after the September 11 attacks, consists of over twenty sculptures made from action figures, plastic vessels, and consumer detritus arranged in post-destruction, architecturally inspired scenes. Elefant (2006) is a column of cascading vertical blinds adorned with plastic tubes, foil, artificial flowers, fabric, and tiny toy soldiers and Indians. For her installation Oil at the 2007 Venice Biennale, she transformed the German Pavilion into a futuristic and morbid Gesamtkunstwerk. She has frequently worked with gallery representative Zwirner, who held her Paris New York Exhibition from August 29 to October 10, 2020, marking her fifth solo exhibition with him since 2010; the exhibition included her early work from the Kunstmuseum Basel and featured her recent "tower" sculptures, inspired by her long-standing fascination with architecture and urban skylines, using vertical structures made of medium-density fiberboard, mirror foil, spray paint, and other media. Genzken's work has significantly influenced art culture through her use of diverse materials such as wood, plaster, concrete, steel, epoxy resin, and household kitchen items, as seen in her "Babies" semblance from 1997. She redefined sculpture by incorporating a broad range of materials and challenged discrimination against sculpture in the 1960s and 1970s, promoting a broader and more inclusive practice. Her work is seen as both contradictory and unpredictable, creating illusions and opening the viewer's imagination. Her first solo exhibition was in 1976 at the Konrad Fischer Gallery in Düsseldorf, and her first exhibition with Galerie Buchholz was in 1986 in Cologne. From November 23, 2013, to March 10, 2014, "Isa Genzken: Retrospective" was exhibited at the Museum of Modern Art, traveling to the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago and the Dallas Museum of Art. Her works are held in international collections, including the Nationalgalerie, West Berlin; Staatsgalerie Stuttgart; Stedelijk Van Abbemuseum, Eindhoven; Rijksmuseum Kroller-Muller, Otterlo; Museum of Modern Art, New York; Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh; Generali Foundation, Vienna; Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Washington, D.C.; Kemper Art Museum, St. Louis; Museum Ludwig, Cologne; Museum Frieder Burda, Baden-Baden; Van Abbemuseum, Eindhoven; Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam; Ruby City, Linda Pace Foundation, San Antonio, TX; and Rose III in Zuccotti Park, NYC. She won the International Art Prize (Cultural Donation of SSK Munich) in 2004 and the Wolfgang-Hahn-Prize (Museum Ludwig, Cologne) in 2002.
